overview: Two of the smallest infectious agents known, distinguished by whether they have a protein coat and what type of nucleic acid they carry.
genZNote: Virus: brings its own hazmat suit (capsid). Viroid: shows up as bare, naked RNA.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: A small infectious agent consisting of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), requiring a host cell to replicate.
aspects.valueB: A small infectious agent consisting solely of a short, circular, single-stranded RNA molecule with no protein coat, infecting only plants.

aspects.label: Protein Coat
aspects.valueA: Present — a capsid (and sometimes an envelope) surrounds the genome.
aspects.valueB: Absent — viroids are "naked" RNA with no protein coat at all.

aspects.label: Genome Type
aspects.valueA: DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded, depending on the virus family.
aspects.valueB: Always a small, circular, single-stranded RNA.

aspects.label: Host Range
aspects.valueA: Infects animals, plants, fungi, bacteria, and archaea depending on the virus.
aspects.valueB: Infects only plants, causing diseases of agricultural crops.

aspects.label: Replication Strategy
aspects.valueA: Encodes at least some proteins to hijack host machinery for replication and assembly.
aspects.valueB: Encodes no proteins at all; relies entirely on host plant RNA polymerase for replication.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Has a protein capsid; infects a broad range of hosts.
aspects.valueB: No protein coat; infects only plants.
